title: The Nihangs
hookLine: blue-robed Sikh orders who keep the old martial traditions alive

cards: Anandpur, in spring, at Hola Mohalla. Out of the dust come riders on horseback, standing in the stirrups at a gallop, spears raised. They wear deep blue robes.

Their turbans are enormous, stacked high, ringed with small steel circles and emblems that flash in the sun. It looks like a scene from three hundred years ago, and in a way it is. These are the Nihangs.
Today, i'll introduce them, then look back on a week of sword and saint.

teach.h: AKALI NIHANGS — THOSE OF THE TIMELESS.
teach.b: The Nihangs are orders of Sikh warriors who keep the Khalsa's old martial life going. They're sometimes called Akali Nihangs, from Akal, the Timeless: the ones who belong to the Timeless.
They wear blue, a color tradition links to Guru Gobind Singh.
They tie the tall turban called a dumalla, often carrying small steel weapons and quoits, the chakkar, in its folds.
They keep horses, train with traditional weapons, and many live a traveling, communal life in camps called chhaunis.
In the eighteenth century, when the Khalsa was fighting to survive, Nihang bands were among its fiercest defenders. Where the name comes from, sources disagree.

Some explain it from a Persian word for a crocodile, fearless in the water. Others from roots meaning without fear, or without attachment. Nobody can settle it, and each explanation says something Nihangs value.
Not every Sikh lives like a Nihang; they're a small part of the panth.
But at Hola Mohalla, the spring gathering tradition traces to Guru Gobind Singh at Anandpur, it's the Nihangs' riding and mock battles that much of the crowd comes to see.

teach.h: A WEEK OF SWORD AND SAINT.
teach.b: Now, the week. The saint-soldier: prayer and courage in one person. Piri, the spirit a little higher.
The kirpan, mercy first. Zafarnama: every other means first. Dharam yudh: fair, even in conflict.
And the Nihangs: the old ways kept. Tomorrow, the last day of this stretch, and the fight the Gurus cared about most.

how: Nihang orders live communally in camps called chhaunis, wear blue with the tall dumalla turban, keep horses and traditional weapons, and gather in great numbers at Hola Mohalla in Anandpur each spring.

games.q: Hola Mohalla at Anandpur. you want to see the old martial traditions of the Khalsa, alive. who do you look for?
o: the Nihangs, in blue, on horseback.
games.why: the Nihang orders still ride, train and gather at Hola Mohalla, keeping the old ways going.

practice: Think of someone who keeps an old way alive: a grandparent who cooks the family dish from memory, a neighbor who mends instead of throwing away, a friend who still writes letters by hand.
Picture them doing it, and notice the patience in it, and what would be lost if nobody did. If you like, choose one old way of your own you'd like to keep going.
